memo:
I have decided that 95 people move to plant roles at plant pay, 15 move to plant roles keeping their current pay, and 15 have their roles eliminated with severance.

The $11.4 million annual saving from the automated work is secured on every path, so the choice turns on one-time cost, ongoing cost and what happens to people. Moving at plant pay is the strongest option. Retraining costs $60,600 per person once, including training pay, and the retraining cost pays back within two years against hiring from outside. It also keeps 95 people employed. Its drawback is pay: a business and financial operations employee's pay falls 39.8%. I do not want to impose that on everyone affected.

Keeping current pay costs $16,560 a person a year for as long as the person holds the plant role. That is more than the hiring saving a retrained person generates, so I limit it to 15 people. It cushions the pay cut for a minority without creating a standing cost of $2.1 million a year.

Eliminating 15 roles is the cheapest path in cash this year, at about $8,902 each in severance. It gives people who do not want to move to plant work a clean exit. I keep it small because it ends the employment of people the Company could retain.

Total one-time cost is about $6.8 million, against $44.1 million of cash above the minimum operating level. The ongoing cost is about $0.25 million a year for the keep-pay group. The board has not set an objective, so this is a balance rather than the maximum on any one measure. Assignments should be communicated early so training starts promptly, and the outside hiring plan for the plants should be reduced by the 95 plus 15 people moved into plant roles.

I have assigned all 125 affected people to the retrain-and-move-at-plant-pay path. The $11.4 million annual saving from the removed work is the same on every path, so the choice turns on what each path costs beyond that.

Compared with elimination, which costs about $8,902 per person in severance, retraining costs $60,600 per person ($15,000 for instruction plus $45,600 in pay and benefits during training). That is about $51,698 more up front per person. The plants hire about 500 people a year from outside, so each internal move fills a role that would otherwise go to an outside hire. The Company states that retraining is paid back within two years against that hiring, and after that the move is ahead. The total one-time cost is $7.6 million, covered by the $44.1 million of cash above the minimum operating level.

I rejected the keep-current-pay path. It has the same $60,600 up-front cost, plus a pay difference of $16,560 a year on average, about $2.1 million a year for all 125. That is pay with no matching work, and it does not pay back on the Company's terms.

Trade-offs: moving at plant pay cuts business and financial operations staff by 39.8% and office staff by 1.5%. This will be hard for some, and some may leave. Elimination is cheaper over the next two years and is the alternative if the board prefers minimum near-term spending or wants to avoid pay cuts of this size. The board has set no objective, so I have judged the choice on long-run cost to the Company. The allocation rule applies the same proportions to both functions, so I could not treat the two groups differently.

I have placed all 125 affected people on the retrain-and-move path at plant-role pay. The work is eliminated on every path, so the $11.4 million a year saving is the same whichever path we choose. The paths differ in cost and in what they return.

Severance costs about $8,902 a person, once, and fills nothing. Retraining costs $60,600 a person ($15,000 instruction plus about $45,600 pay and benefits during training), once. But each retrained person fills a plant role we would otherwise fill by hiring from outside, and the retraining cost pays back against that hiring in two years. Over a horizon of several years, moving people is clearly worth more than severance, and the 125 moves fit within the roughly 500 plant hires we make each year.

Keeping current pay is the weakest option. It costs the same retraining sum plus $16,560 a person a year, or $2.1 million a year for 125 people. That top-up eats most of the hiring benefit, so payback stretches to roughly four to five years. I have not chosen it.

Using the same proportion for both functions, the path lands hardest on business and financial operations, where pay falls by 39.8%, while office and administrative support falls by only 1.5%. This is a real hardship, and it creates a risk that some of the 55 business staff leave before the move pays back. I recommend monitoring resignations in that group closely over the first year, and planning for a targeted severance fallback if attrition rises above what the plant roles can absorb. I have not split the group, because the board's instruction applies one proportion to both functions.

The board has not set an objective, so I have chosen on cost and recovery over the medium term. Severance is the lower-cost choice in year one, and I accept that trade-off.

I have placed 100 of the 125 affected people in plant roles at plant pay and eliminated 25 roles with severance. No one is placed on the keep-current-pay path.

The plants hire about 500 people a year from outside, so 100 internal moves can fill roles the Company would otherwise recruit for. Each move costs $60,600 once: $15,000 of instruction and materials, plus $45,600 of pay and benefits during six months of training. The retraining cost pays back in about two years against outside hiring. The $11.4 million annual saving from the automated work is secured on every path, so the choice turns on these one-time costs and on people's jobs.

The keep-current-pay path adds about $16,560 per person a year, or $2.1 million a year across 125 people, with no payback. It would also leave people earning well above plant colleagues doing the same work, so I have rejected it.

Eliminating roles is the cheapest path at about $8,900 per person in severance. I have kept 25 eliminations for two reasons. Business and financial operations staff would take a 39.8% pay cut on a plant move, so some of them may choose to leave, and severance gives them a clean exit. Keeping some severance capacity also reduces the risk of the transfer program being overloaded. Office staff would see only a 1.5% reduction.

Total one-time cost is about $6.3 million, well within the $44.1 million of cash above the minimum operating level. The board has not set an objective, so this mix is my judgment: it favors redeployment and job retention while limiting cost. The main risk is attrition among business staff after the pay cut. I recommend monitoring that closely over the training period and reviewing the split if resignations rise.

Proportions apply equally to both functions, so the split is roughly 56 percent office and administrative support and 44 percent business and financial operations.

The $11.4 million a year saving from the AI-driven work change is achieved on every path, so this decision turns on the one-time and ongoing costs of each path and on the people affected. The board has not set an objective, so I have weighed cost against retention without maximizing either.

I set move_keep_pay to zero. It adds about $2.1 million a year in pay differences for all 125 people, on top of the same retraining cost as the move_plant_pay path. It buys no hiring benefit that move_plant_pay does not already give, so it is the weakest economic choice, and I would only use it if the board places a high value on avoiding any pay reduction.

I split the remaining people between eliminate (50) and move_plant_pay (75). Eliminate is the cheapest route at about $8,900 a person in severance, or $0.4 million for 50 people. Move_plant_pay costs about $60,600 a person once (retraining plus training pay), or $4.5 million for 75 people, and avoids outside hiring for plant roles the Company fills anyway; the retraining cost alone pays back in two years. Total one-time cost is about $5.0 million, well within the $44.1 million of cash above the minimum.

The 60/40 split applies to both functions: about 42 and 28 in office and administrative support, and 33 and 22 in business and financial operations. For office staff the plant-role pay cut is small, $839 a year (1.5%). For business and financial staff it is large, $36,569 a year (39.8%), and some may decline or leave. That risk should be monitored, and the board may wish to revisit the split if acceptance is low.

The board should note that the move path's payback depends on the plants continuing to hire about 500 people a year, and that the training-pay cost is not covered by the two-year payback figure.

I have assigned all 125 affected people to retraining and a move into a plant role at plant-role pay.

The $11.4 million annual saving from the automated work is the same on every path, so the choice turns on the one-time and ongoing costs that differ between paths. Elimination is the cheapest up front, at $1.1 million of severance. But the plants hire about 500 people a year, and each retrained person fills a role the Company would otherwise fill by hiring from outside. The $15,000 retraining cost pays back within two years against that hiring, so moving people is cheaper than eliminating them over any horizon beyond that. The one-time cost of this path is $7.6 million: $1.9 million of retraining and $5.7 million of pay and benefits during training. That is covered by the $44.1 million of cash above the minimum operating level, and it leaves the $300 million revolver undrawn.

Keeping current pay costs about $2.1 million a year, or $16,560 per person, for no operational return, because the person still fills a plant role that would otherwise be filled from outside. I have therefore not chosen it.

The main cost of this decision falls on the 55 business and financial operations staff, whose pay falls by 40%, and on the 70 office staff, whose pay falls by 1.5%. The board should be aware of that. It may wish to address it through transition support or by revisiting the keep-pay path for those most affected. This decision does not meet that need, and it is a judgment the board has not asked me to make in isolation.

Retaining 125 people in the Company, rather than cutting them, also keeps in-house the skills and service knowledge the plants need.

All 125 affected people are retrained and moved into plant roles at plant-role pay. The board has set no objective, so I weighed cost, the people affected and the Company's needs together.

Cost. Moving at plant pay is roughly neutral on ongoing cost compared with elimination. The plants hire about 500 people a year into these roles anyway, so a transferred employee at $55,211 replaces an outside hire at the same rate, and the former role's pay ends either way. The extra cost is one-time: about $60,600 a person for retraining and training-period pay, against $8,902 severance. Across 125 people that is roughly $7.6 million gross, or about $6.5 million more than elimination in year one. The $15,000 retraining cost pays back within two years against outside hiring.

Keeping current pay costs $2.1 million a year for no offsetting benefit, since the plant role is filled whichever path is chosen. I rejected it.

Elimination is the cheapest path at $1.1 million, but it ends 125 jobs and gives the Company no skilled plant workers.

Concerns. Plant pay is a 1.5% cut for office and administrative staff and a 39.8% cut, $36,569 a year, for business and financial operations staff. That is severe. The path is chosen by function proportion, so I cannot tailor it. I ask management to consider transition support for the business and financial operations group, and to report back on how many accept and how many leave. If cash becomes the priority, moving some people to elimination is the lever, at a lower one-time cost.

The board has not set an objective, so I weighed the three paths on cost, on people's jobs and pay, and on the Company's need for plant labour.

I rejected the keep-pay path. It adds $2.1 million a year for as long as the people hold plant roles, which is a recurring cost on a business that already returns 90% of net income to shareholders. It also leaves people in plant roles paid well above colleagues doing the same work.

I chose the plant-pay move for most of the group, 80 people. It keeps them employed and fills plant openings that would otherwise go to outside hires. Its cost is one-time: about $60,600 a person, or roughly $4.8 million in total, which is within the $44.1 million of cash above the minimum. The Company's own estimate is that the retraining cost pays back in two years against hiring from outside. The pay effect is uneven. Office and administrative staff lose about 1.5% of pay, which is small. Business and financial staff lose about 40%, which is severe, and I want the board to see that clearly.

I chose elimination for the remaining 45 people. Severance is about $8,902 a person, roughly $0.4 million in total, and it ends their pay. That is a real hardship, but it is a one-time cost and avoids a large pay cut for people who cannot be placed.

The split follows the constraint that both functions move in the same proportion, so about 64% of each function takes the plant move. The savings of $11.4 million a year are the same on every path.

Before the first moves, HR should check whether the 40% pay cut for business and financial staff can be reduced, for example through a longer phase-in or a retention allowance. Any such cost would reduce the cash available for the other paths.

Moving at plant pay costs the same one-time sum with no ongoing gap, and the pack states the $15,000 retraining cost is paid back within two years compared with hiring from outside. I therefore assign 75 to move_plant_pay and 50 to eliminate. One-time cost is about $4.5 million for retraining and $0.4 million for severance, well within the $44.1 million of cash above the minimum.

Two cautions. Business and financial staff moving at plant pay take a 39.8% pay cut, a serious hardship, and the board should consider whether it accepts that. Also, the two-year payback covers only the $15,000 instruction cost. The $45,600 training pay is not recovered by the figures given, so the case for retraining rests on avoided hiring, which I have not verified. Before proceeding, I recommend the board confirm the avoided hiring cost and review the pay reduction.

The board has set no objective, so I chose a mix that keeps most of the 125 people employed, fills plant roles the Company would otherwise recruit for, and stays well within the $44.1 million of cash above the minimum.

Keeping current pay for 25 people costs $16,560 a person a year, or about $414,000 a year, on top of their retraining. It protects those, mainly in business and financial operations, whose pay would otherwise fall by 39.8%.

I kept 15 on severance as a hedge against slow retraining, since people take six months to work independently, and as a certain, low-cost exit for anyone whose role does not translate to the plants.

A board focused on lowest cost in the first year would move more people toward elimination. A board focused on pay protection would move more people toward keeping current pay. I have taken a middle course that favours keeping people in the Company.
